newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran economy recovers on oil but reforms needed.
newsitem.headline: Iran economy recovers on oil but reforms needed.

text.p: Iran's sluggish economy is perking up as windfall petrodollars ease foreign debt pressures.
But real sustained growth could be threatened by U.S. sanctions and stalled reforms, diplomats and officials said on Wednesday.
An oil price rally since last June is forecast to earn Iran a bonus of up to $3.5 billion in the current Iranian year which ends on March 20, and $2.5 billion next year, diplomats said.
Oil receipts for the current year were forecast at $15.99 billion and Oil Minister Gholamreza Aghazadeh has already predicted $18 billion for next year.
"Overall the economic situation has improved since the summer. Now with the oil price surge the country will be able to contain its foreign debt problem," a Western diplomat said.
"Iran has achieved good progress in repayments and inflation and growth rates are (improved), at least officially," he added.
IMF Middle East head Paul Chabrier last month predicted the Iranian economy would grow four percent in the year to March, up from 3.5 percent in the previous year.

The oil price rally has given Tehran a breathing space from a gruelling debt repayment schedule which led in 1994 to the Iranian government rescheduling more than $10 billion in foreign debt and allowed a buildup in hard currency reserves.
Higher receipts had also led a more confident central bank to approach international financiers to seek further loans on a 8.5-year repayment basis rather than the usual five years.
Iran's foreign debt soared to more than $30 billion by the early 1990s caused by lax control over an explosive import bill after the end of its eight-year war with Iraq in 1988.

Latest figures released by the Central Bank show the country's rescheduled repayment obligations at $7.15 billion in 1997-98, $4.19 billion in 1998-99, falling to $2.62 billion in 1999-2000 and just $637 million in 2000-2001.
These repayments are expected to keep domestic hard currency allocations for large projects at a subdued level.
"The country is still in a very tight situation...It can't finance large projects," one diplomat said.

The boost in hard currency income and a strict clampdown on black market money changers has also allowed Iran to put some reins on the rial which in 1995 came close to a free-fall when U.S. President Bill Clinton announced sanctions against Tehran.
Diplomats estimated annual inflation in the capital at 30 percent compared to 50 percent in the first half of 1996. Official figures put inflation at about 25 percent.
The rial was quoted on the illegal black market on Wednesday at 4,600 to the U.S. dollar, compared to the official rate of 3,000, and the 4,900 level reached late last year.

This disparity would hinder any attempt in the coming Iranian year to unify the exchange rates and make the rial fully convertible. Those policies were central parts of Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani's economic reform programme but were abandoned in 1995, diplomats said.

Direct foreign investment in the Islamic republic was still being deterred by U.S. trade sanctions and a lack of a basic law governing outside investment including the right to repatriate earnings, diplomats said.

The government's privatisation process had slowed, even privatised firms remained still largely owned by state officials and the powerful bazaar merchants choked any meaningful reform, diplomats said.
"Economic reforms are slow to come up...The bazaaris don't want to hear about the opening up of the economy if that means the bazaaris have less to import," one said.
"Full convertibility, floating exchange rates and freer trade are laudable objectives but it's not got a snowball's chance in hell," another said.
Iranian oil experts were also cautious on the outlook for oil prices which still account for close to 90 percent of government export earnings.

"We felt that we should have adopted the $16.50 price in the second five-year plan (1995-2000)," one expert said, adding the $17.50 base in next year's budget may prove too bullish because of a potential downturn in oil demand from April to June.
